newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORMER S.AFRICA POLICY-MAKER SLAMS RATE POLICY.
newsitem.headline: FORMER S.AFRICA POLICY-MAKER SLAMS RATE POLICY.

text.p: A co-author of South Africa's macro-economic strategy for post-apartheid economic growth has accused central bank governor Chris Stals of undermining the government's flagship recovery plan.

Iraj Abedian, an associate professor of economics at the University of Cape Town, said in an interview that Stals had maintained the South African Reserve Bank's key interest rate at 17 percent for far too long.
"Chris Stals hasn't been growth friendly or even patriotic to the South African economy. His idiosyncratic obsession with inflation is damaging the economy," he said.
Abedian coordinated a team that helped the Finance Ministry draft the Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy, known as Gear, that was published last June.

The strategy imposes a mix of fiscal discipline, deficit reduction, export promotion and labour restraint to boost growth to six percent a year by the end of the century and significantly reverse the decline in employment.
Stals hiked the bank's key interest rate to 17 percent in November last year, pushing the prime rate charged by commercial banks to 20.25 percent.
Citing inflation that tested 10 percent year-on-year in April before dropping back to the current level of 8.8 percent, Stals has so far declined to bow to pressure to cut the rate.

He said in July, however, the falling inflation rate as well as a decline in the rate of money supply growth to 12.79 percent in June and a slight drop in the stubbornly high rate of growth in personal credit extension at 16.39 percent augured well for a cut this year.
"Stals is paranoid about inflation, but he should not be allowed to hold the economy hostage to his paranoia," said Abedian.
"He has terribly undermined the credibility of Gear. He is flying in the face of every single professional economic analyst in the country," he said.
He said monetary policy should be set by a board of governors chaired by Stals and including independent economists.

South Africa's economy contracted by an annualised 0.8 percent quarter-on-quarter in the first quarter of 1997 and economists are divided on whether to expect a second quarter of negative growth when the figure is announced later this month.
Most economists define a recession as two consecutive quarters of negative growth.

The Business Day newspaper quoted Finance Director General Maria Ramos as telling a conference in Johannesburg earlier this week that the government had revised its growth estimate for 1997 down from 2.9 percent to 2.2 percent.
ING Barings economist Nick Barnardt echoed Abedian's concern that Stals was stifling growth, telling Reuters:
"We are sacrificing a bit more growth than is necessary. Inflation of seven to eight percent is low enough and that's already in the bag.
"The question is, do you loosen up by lowering the interest rate or by letting the rand depreciate, which will boost export earnings," he said.

Barnardt said his own view was that South Africa should lift remaining exchange controls within the next six months and let the rand, which traded at 4.66 to the dollar on Wednesday, find its own level.
